units: the writer answers a complaint from the reader about poor sleep
the writer has asked a caregiver at a care center
the recommendations are sorted into three separate groups
the first group covers what one eats in the evening
a lack of iron is presented as a source of lasting weariness
the second group deals with physical activity and loosening exercises
the third group describes the conditions of the bedroom
the caregiver advises seeking help if the spells come back
the writer asks for a reply about the measures tried
text: You wrote that your evenings are restless and that sleep keeps slipping away from you. I put the question to a nurse at the care center I go to, and she arranges her advice under three separate headings. The first is about what you eat late in the day: no heavy meals before bed, and she reminded me that a shortage of iron feeds a stubborn, lingering tiredness. The second is about moving: walk every afternoon, loosen the shoulders once evening arrives, avoid violent exertion as night approaches. The third heading is the bedroom itself, which she wants cool, dark, quiet, with no screen glowing anywhere. One remark of hers has stayed with me since. If the dizzy spells or the chills return, don't wait them out, seek attention quickly. Write and tell me what you have attempted, and I will say whether it matches her description.

units: a patient being interviewed describes the stages of her recovery
the first sensation mentioned is a heaviness in the limbs
a state of turned stomach then arrives in waves
the first week felt endless to her
the second week went by almost unnoticed
quiet and dim light helped her get better
a caregiver kneaded the back of her neck at the end of the day
a slow-healing wound on her arm worried her more than her diagnosis
she advises asking nothing of oneself
text: What comes first? The patient we spoke with describes a dull heaviness, as though her arms and legs had doubled in weight. And after that? Nausea, she says, a wave that rises and pulls back without warning. Does that stage last? She hesitates, then answers that the first week felt endless, while the second slipped by almost without a trace. What eased it? Quiet, dim light, and the hand of a nurse's aide who came at dusk to knead the back of her neck. And the nights? Sleep returned in pieces, never in one whole stretch. Was she afraid she would not recover? She admits that a wound on her arm was slow to close, and that this small thing worried her more than the whole diagnosis. What does she advise in the end? Ask nothing of yourself, and take slowness as an ally rather than an enemy.

units: a sports doctor explains a chain of causes to his patient
an unprepared muscle stays cold and short on suppleness
a cold fiber tears more easily during a sudden lengthening
the tear brings on a local inflammatory reaction
the inflammation draws in blood and sets off the pain
the patient asks about the swelling of his knee
the swelling follows from the same chain
cold applied to the area eases the phenomenon
loading the joint too soon delays the healing
text: The sports doctor walks his patient through the chain of events. Skipping the warm-up, he explains, leaves the muscle fibers cold and short on stretch. The patient wants to know what that changes in practice. A cold fiber handles a sudden lengthening badly, the doctor answers, and tears without much resistance. The tear then sets off inflammation right at that spot, and the inflammation pulls blood in, which is where the pain comes from. The patient is puzzled by the swelling that has come up around his knee. Same mechanism, the doctor tells him, and a cold pack held against the area will settle it down. A muscle that has been properly prepared takes those jolts without giving way. He finishes with a warning: load the joint too soon and the healing drags on and on. Build the training back up step by step.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: in the past minor wounds killed patients with no other illness
practitioners saw fever and discharge without understanding the source
infection was then judged unavoidable
observers noticed a difference between the treatment rooms
the rooms where hands went unwashed lost more patients
the measure adopted was the cleaning of hands and instruments
this measure was poorly received at first by the caregivers
the death records ended up convincing them
this rule remains a foundation of care
text: There was a time when minor wounds carried off patients who had nothing else wrong with them. Doctors watched the fever climb, the chills set in, the wound run, and could not name what tied these things together. The trouble lay in a belief: infection was taken as unavoidable, almost part of the natural order. Patient observers eventually caught a pattern across the wards, since the rooms where hands went unwashed lost more of the sick than the rest. The remedy was severe in its plainness. Wash the hands, scrub the instruments clean, before every single procedure. Resistance ran high, because such a demand pointed a finger at the caregivers themselves. The death counts won the argument in the end, and the losses began to fall. That modest rule still holds as one of the foundations of care.

units: two close sensations are often confused with each other
one gives the illusion that the room is turning
the other feels like an inner collapse without turning
the first has its origin in the inner ear
the inner ear tells the brain how the head is tilted
the second comes from a short drop in blood supply to the brain
faced with the first one should sit down and stare at a fixed point
faced with the second one should lie down and raise the legs
a repeat of these episodes calls for a medical examination
text: Two neighboring sensations get mixed up all the time: vertigo and faintness. With vertigo the whole room seems to spin around you, while faintness feels more like an inner collapse, with no spinning at all. Vertigo most often starts in the inner ear, the part that reports to the brain on how the head is tilted. Faintness, for its part, comes from a brief drop in the blood supply reaching the brain. The useful response differs in each case, and bystanders who confuse the two delay the appropriate reaction. When vertigo strikes, sit down, lock your eyes on something motionless, and hold the neck still. When faintness comes on, lie down and raise the legs so that blood flows back toward the head. One isolated episode is hardly alarming, but repeated recurrences deserve a full medical examination.

units: the narrator recounts a stay at a treatment center
the treatments included bubbling baths and clay wraps
a therapist kneaded his back with vigor
he describes the other guests he met there
a teenager had been sent there by his lung doctor
the food lacked taste but was served with solemnity
he slept better than he had in a very long time
he left lighter and convinced that rest is something one learns
text: Alright, let me tell you about my week at the treatment center, because it was worth the trip. The treatments first: bubbling baths, clay wraps, and a therapist who worked my back over until I laughed from the pain. Then the other guests: a former swimmer who talked nonstop, a retired woman who knew every hallway, a teenager sent there by his lung doctor and sulking about it. Then the meals: bland, honestly, though served with a seriousness that made the blandness almost ceremonial. And then the nights: I slept the way I hadn't slept in ages, no sudden jolting awake, none of that knot sitting in the throat. The thick quiet of the corridors surely had something to do with it. I came home lighter, a bit ridiculous in a bathrobe that was far too short, and convinced that rest is something you learn.

units: the first check concerns the state of the shoes
a worn sole upsets the footing and strains the knees
a warm-up of wide movements comes before the run
the calves and the thighs are loosened without forcing
the start is at a pace that allows talking
the speed rises only past the first third of the route
the stop must be gradual and followed by walking
a lukewarm shower relaxes the muscles on getting home
a sharp pain in a knee means giving up the next session
text: Start with your shoes: a worn sole throws the stride off balance and wears the knees out over time. Then devote a dozen or so wide swinging movements to the warm-up, enough to raise the heart rate gradually rather than abruptly. Stretch the calves and the thighs, and never force a joint that feels stiff. Set off at an easy pace, one you could sustain while talking out loud. Pick the speed up only past the first third of the route. At the finish, don't stop dead: keep walking, let the breathing settle, drink in small spaced sips. Tell someone your intended route if you head out alone as evening falls. Once home, a lukewarm shower is enough to soothe the muscles. Drink again half an hour afterward. If a sharp pain shows up in a knee, skip the following session and have it examined.

units: seats are short in the waiting room of a clinic
the closing of a nearby practice moved its clientele to this place
the wait before an appointment has grown longer
the visits have become shorter
unanswered questions bring the patients back one more time
a caregiver says she recognizes the same faces too often
mild disorders worsen for want of steady follow-up
management announces two more practitioners in the warm season
text: Seats have been short in the clinic waiting room since autumn. The practice down the street shut its doors and pushed a whole clientele in here, and the effect spread outward from there. Appointments drift further off, so visits get shorter; shorter visits leave questions hanging, so patients come back again. A mother who came in for her son leaves with one question out of three answered. A nurse's aide talks about faces she recognizes far too often. Without steady follow-up, mild problems worsen quietly: a deficiency left untreated, a wound that refuses to close, a blood pressure climbing with no alarm. Management says two more doctors will arrive when the warm season comes. Until then, care goes to whoever needs it most, and everyone senses that the backlog will be paid for later.

units: a first-aid kit fits in a hard case closed with a strap
the main difficulty comes from the mess and not from the contents
one searches inside it at a moment when the hands are shaking
the solution is to split the supplies into labeled compartments
the first compartment holds what is needed to clean a wound
the second gathers dressings wraps and round-tipped scissors
the third holds gloves an emergency blanket and a medical book
the book lists the current treatments and the allergies
the kit is placed near the entrance so a visitor can find it
text: A well-planned first-aid kit fits inside a hard case that closes with a strap. The usual trouble is not what goes into it but the mess that builds up inside, since you end up digging through it exactly when your hands are shaking. The remedy is to distribute the supplies among clearly labeled compartments. The first one holds sterile pads and the saline for cleaning out a wound. The second keeps dressings in several sizes, elastic wraps, and a pair of round-tipped scissors. The third stores disposable gloves, a folded emergency blanket, and a small book that lists the treatments being taken along with any known allergies. A recent prescription can be slipped in alongside it. Kept near the front door, the case stays within reach even for a visitor who does not know the place.

units: two directions of care are set against each other
the first acts once the illness has declared itself
its effectiveness is easily observed
the second steps in before the disorder appears
its results stay invisible because they consist of illnesses avoided
this difference in visibility explains the gap in funding
the writer holds that preventing costs less and spares suffering
the writer asks that both directions be funded equally
text: We are too quick to set the medicine that repairs against the medicine that prevents, as if one had to hand its resources over to the other. The first steps in once the illness has declared itself: it operates, prescribes, relieves, and its results are easy to measure. The second works before any disorder appears, and what it achieves stays out of sight, since it consists of illnesses that never happened. That imbalance in visibility explains the imbalance in the budgets. Repair can be seen, prevention cannot. Still, it deserves saying plainly that prevention costs less and spares whole stretches of suffering, whereas repair tends to arrive late in the day. Our health institutions ought to fund both paths with the same steadiness, instead of treating the second as an optional add-on.
